title: GDC Standards for the Dental Team
blurb: The nine principles every registrant must follow, what each one means for a dental nurse, and why honesty runs through them all.
question: At the end of a busy session a colleague asks you to tick the autoclave log for a cycle you didn't see run, 'just so the paperwork is complete'. Which GDC principles are involved, and what should you do?

teach.body: The General Dental Council (GDC) regulates the dental team in the UK to protect the public. Its Standards for the Dental Team set out nine principles that every registered professional must follow, including dental nurses. Each principle starts with what patients can expect, then lists the standards you must meet. As a student dental nurse you are expected to work to them now. A serious or repeated breach can lead to a fitness to practise investigation and put your registration at risk.

teach.intro: Polite Children Can Imitate Cats, Cows, Kangaroos, Rabbits and Bears.
teach.word: P C C I C C K R B

letters.word: Have a clear and effective complaints procedure
Work with colleagues in a way that is in patients' best interests
Maintain, develop and work within your professional knowledge and skills
Raise concerns if patients are at risk
Make sure your personal behaviour maintains confidence in you and the dental profession

teach.caption: Learn them in order: exam questions often name a scenario and ask which principle it engages.

teach.h: What each principle means for you
head: Principle
For a dental nurse
rows: Dignity, honesty, fairness; money never sways care; indemnity in place
Plain words, listen, check understanding, meet communication needs
Support the clinician; spot doubt; tell the dentist if a patient wants to stop
Keep records accurate and secure; share only on a need-to-know basis
Know the practice procedure; respond politely and pass it on promptly
Respect, teamwork, delegate and accept tasks only within scope
Stay in scope, do your CPD, only do what you are trained for
Speak up about risk to patients, even about a senior colleague
Act with integrity at work, outside work and online

teach.caption: The Standards use both words deliberately. Read questions carefully for which one applies.

teach.body: Most real-life breaches come down to honesty. Never record something you did not do or see, such as a sterilisation check or a decontamination cycle. If a patient overpays, tell them and refund it. Give references that are honest and fair. If you are asked about a colleague in an investigation, describe only what you personally saw, not gossip or opinion. A falsified log may look like paperwork, but it hides a risk to patients and breaks Principle 1 (honesty and integrity) and Principle 9 at once.

steps.label: Pause
steps.sub: Don't sign or tick under pressure

steps.label: Decline politely
steps.sub: 'I can only record what I saw'

steps.label: Put it right
steps.sub: If a check was missed, it needs redoing, not ticking

teach.text: The Standards don't stop at the practice door. Principle 9 covers your personal life and online behaviour too, so a drunken social media post or a criminal caution can become a GDC matter.

items: Nine principles: patients first, communicate, consent, information, complaints, colleagues, knowledge and skills, raise concerns, behaviour.
'Must' is compulsory; 'should' is expected unless you can justify departing from it.
Never falsify a record or log. Decline, put it right and raise the concern.
Be honest with money, references and in investigations: report only what you saw.
The Standards apply at work, outside work and online.

summary: You can now list the GDC's nine principles in order, explain what each means for a dental nurse, tell 'must' from 'should', and handle the classic honesty scenarios: a falsified log, an overpayment, a reference and an investigation.

A.q: A colleague asks you to sign the decontamination log for a cycle you did not witness. What should you do?
options: Sign it, as the cycle almost certainly ran
Sign it, adding a note that you didn't see it
Decline, as records must show what you saw
Ask the receptionist to sign instead
A.why: A record must reflect what actually happened. Signing for something you did not witness is falsifying a record and could hide a risk to patients.

whyNot.0: 'Probably' is not good enough: the log exists to prove the cycle ran correctly.
whyNot.1: Your signature still certifies a cycle you didn't see; a log entry must be made by the person who witnessed it.
whyNot.3: Passing it to someone else who also didn't witness it is still falsification.

A.q: Which of these is one of the nine principles in the GDC Standards for the Dental Team?

whyNot.1: You work under the dentist's direction, but you must still raise concerns if patients are at risk.
whyNot.2: Fair care means meeting each patient's needs, which is not the same as treating everyone identically.
whyNot.3: Principle 1 says patients' interests come before money or the business.

A.q: A patient overpays by £20 at reception and leaves without noticing. What is the most professional action?
options: Keep it on file in case they ask for it
Put it towards their next visit
Wait and see if they notice
Contact the patient and refund it
A.why: Honesty in financial dealings is part of putting patients' interests first. Tell the patient and correct the payment.

whyNot.0: Holding their money without telling them is not honest.
whyNot.1: The patient hasn't agreed to a credit, so this decision isn't yours to make.
whyNot.2: Relying on the patient to spot your error is not acting with integrity.

B.q: In the GDC Standards, what does the word 'should' indicate?
options: A legal duty with no exceptions
Expected unless you can justify otherwise
Guidance for dentists but not for nurses
An optional suggestion you can ignore
B.why: 'Should' describes expected practice. You may depart from it only with good reason, and you must be able to justify why.

whyNot.2: The Standards apply to every registrant, including dental nurses.
whyNot.3: It isn't optional: departing from it needs a justification.

B.q: You are asked for a reference for a former colleague who was often late. What does the GDC expect?
options: Give an honest and fair account
Exaggerate to help them move on
B.why: References must be honest and fair, based on what you know.

whyNot.0: You may decline, but refusing doesn't meet the duty to be honest and fair when you do give one.
whyNot.1: Deliberately hiding relevant facts makes the reference misleading.
whyNot.3: Exaggeration is dishonest and could put patients at risk.

B.q: A nurse posts offensive comments about patients online in her own time. Which principle is most directly engaged?
B.why: Principle 9 requires your personal behaviour, including online and outside work, to maintain confidence in you and the profession.

whyNot.0: Principle 6 is about teamwork in patients' best interests.
whyNot.1: Principle 2 covers communication with patients during care.
whyNot.2: Principle 5 is about having a clear complaints procedure.

C.q: During a practice investigation you are asked about a colleague's conduct. What is the professional approach?
options: Describe only what you saw yourself
Repeat what other staff have told you
Decline to take any part at all
Give your honest view of their character
C.why: Stick to facts you personally observed. Hearsay and opinion are unfair and unreliable.

whyNot.1: Second-hand accounts are hearsay; others can give their own evidence.
whyNot.2: You should cooperate with a legitimate investigation.
whyNot.3: Opinions about character are not evidence of conduct.

C.q: Which principle covers doing your CPD and only carrying out tasks you are trained for?
options: Raise concerns if patients are at risk
C.why: Principle 7 is 'Maintain, develop and work within your professional knowledge and skills'.

whyNot.0: Principle 1 is about dignity, honesty and putting patients before money.
whyNot.1: Principle 8 is about speaking up when patients are at risk.

C.q: Which of these is NOT one of the nine GDC principles?
options: Raise concerns if patients are at risk
C.why: Appraisal is good practice, but it is not one of the nine principles.

reteach.title: The Standards as a promise to patients
reteach.question: Imagine a patient reading the poster in your waiting room. What are they being promised, and what does that ask of you?

blocks.body: Each principle is really a promise. The patient is told: you'll come first, we'll explain things clearly, we'll ask your permission, we'll keep your details safe, we'll listen if you complain, the team will work together for you, we'll only do what we're trained to do, we'll speak up if something's wrong, and we'll behave in a way you can trust. Your job is to keep every one of those promises.

blocks.caption: Row one is about the patient in the chair; row two about information and teamwork; row three about you as a professional.

rows.label: Leaving a day list on the reception desk
Ignoring a colleague who skips hand hygiene
Telling a patient off for asking questions

explain.h: Principles 1 to 3: the patient in the chair
explain.body: Put patients' interests first (dignity, honesty, fairness, no gifts swaying care), communicate effectively (plain language, listening, checking understanding) and obtain valid consent (voluntary, informed, with capacity).

test.q: A patient is told they must have treatment today because the diary is full next month. Which principle is most at risk?
test.why: Pressure undermines voluntary consent, which is Principle 3.

whyNot.0: No complaint has been made here.
whyNot.2: Nobody is working beyond their training.
whyNot.3: No patient information is being misused.

explain.body: Maintain and protect patients' information (accurate, secure records and confidentiality), have a clear and effective complaints procedure, and work with colleagues in patients' best interests (respect, good teamwork, appropriate delegation).

test.q: A patient's record is left open on an unattended reception screen. Which principle does this breach?
test.why: Principle 4 requires you to maintain and protect patients' information, including on screens.

whyNot.1: Principle 9 concerns personal conduct rather than information security.
whyNot.2: Principle 2 is about how you communicate with patients.

explain.h: Principles 7 to 9: you as a professional
explain.body: Maintain, develop and work within your professional knowledge and skills (scope, training, CPD), raise concerns if patients are at risk, and make sure your personal behaviour maintains confidence in you and the profession, including outside work.

test.q: You notice the dentist regularly reusing single-use items. Which principle tells you to act?
test.why: Principle 8 requires you to raise concerns when patients are at risk, whoever the colleague is.

whyNot.1: Complaints come from patients; this is a safety concern you must raise.
whyNot.2: Patients' interests are involved, but the specific duty to speak up is Principle 8.
whyNot.3: This is about patient safety, not communication.

explain.body: Only record what you did or saw. Missed checks are redone, never ticked off. Refund overpayments, write fair references and give only first-hand facts in investigations.

steps.label: Decline
steps.sub: Don't sign for what you didn't see

test.q: The daily autoclave test was missed this morning. A colleague suggests writing it in as done. What is correct?
options: Write it in, as the machine is new
Leave the log blank and say nothing
Write it in, then tell the manager at lunchtime
Run the test now and record it honestly
test.why: Carry out the check and record what actually happened, with the real time. Never falsify a log.

whyNot.0: A new machine still needs its tests; writing it in is falsification.
whyNot.1: Saying nothing leaves a safety gap unaddressed.
whyNot.2: Falsifying first and confessing later is still falsifying.
